title_original: Stephen Shore: “The World Would Be a Better Place if Everyone Really Paid Attention”
editorial_title_zh: Stephen Shore：“如果每个人都能真正专心致志，世界将会变得更好”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在《The Mental Image》中，斯蒂芬·肖尔（Stephen Shore）终于用文字梳理了他私下承载了40年的传统——一张照片不仅可以定格一个场景，还能留下心灵的痕迹。L’article Stephen Shore: “The World Would Be a Better Place if Everyone Really Paid Attention” est…

article_text:
The desert at Big Bend National Park does not give a photographer much to hold onto: no trees to break the horizon, no telephone poles to organise the eye, nothing but heat rising off dry ground and a sky as cloudless as a wall. It was here, in 1987, that Stephen Shore set up his 8×10 camera and made two photographs of the same landscape, under the same light and at the same exposure. Nothing in the scene had changed. What changed was what Shore was seeing. In one photograph, he held the horizon in his mind as a flat line; in the other, he concentrated on its depth – the sheer distance folding out toward the vanishing point. The camera had not moved, yet experienced photographers could see a difference between the two images. What, exactly, had happened between those exposures, in the emptiest of landscapes, where nothing changed but the photographer’s mind?

Since American Surfaces and Uncommon Places , Shore has made a practice of looking at the ordinary until it becomes newly strange. While writing The Nature of Photographs , he hesitated to describe the tradition behind this way of seeing. Now, approaching seventy-nine, he has decided to take the risk. “I don’t care if people think it’s a little off the wall,” he says.

The tradition he describes is not so much a school of thought as a thread running quietly through American photography – from Stieglitz and Weston through Adams, Minor White, Paul Caponigro and Frederick Sommer. Weston called it “previsualizing,” but Shore is interested in what might happen before the shutter: in the photographer’s awareness of seeing photographically, and in the possibility that this awareness itself leaves a trace.

After Big Bend, Shore called Sommer, who told him he understood what had happened. “Minor White thinks it’s mystical, but it’s physics,” he said. That idea lingers through the book. Shore does not know what the physics might be; he points instead to the interstitial system – a network of fluid-filled spaces in the body – as an example of something physical that may exist before we have the language to describe it. “I’m not going to pretend I understand how this works,” he says. Asked whether he can see the difference himself, his answer comes without hesitation: yes.

Then the past unexpectedly supplied its own evidence. About two weeks after Shore repeated the experiment with a student, photographing the same brick wall under identical conditions, Eleanor Caponigro sent him a story about the composer Ernest Bloch and Stieglitz. In 1917, Bloch challenged Stieglitz’s claim that photography was an art. Stieglitz invited him to the studio, and they made exactly the same picture. That evening, in the red darkroom light, they processed their prints in the same tray and watched the images rise from the blank paper, side by side. Bloch could see immediately. His was “dull and drab”; Stieglitz’s was “alive.” Shore realised that the experiment he had just performed had already unfolded once before, nearly a century earlier. The coincidence feels almost like another experiment – evidence arriving from the past.

The Mental Image is full of attempts to give physical form to what usually remains invisible: the moment when an intention becomes a choice, when looking becomes seeing, when experience enters the photograph. But Shore is careful about the limits of what he knows. The effect, he argues, depends on fluency – on spending enough time with a camera and the materials of photography that thought becomes embodied. He compares it to a basketball player imagining a free throw: visualisation matters because the body already knows what it is being asked to do. “Some of the exercises in the book only work once there’s a foundation of real technical material and formal experience,” he says.

The view camera makes this argument physical: heavy, slow and demanding. Shore places a coin on the ground to mark the tripod’s exact position before walking back to retrieve the camera; when he returns, the tiny marker allows him to reconstruct it. The camera weighs around seven kilograms; setting it up means moving through a sequence of physical decisions before the picture can exist. “Every decision becomes physical,” Shore says. The camera does not disappear into photographing; it makes the act impossible to ignore.

Shore has spent more than forty years teaching, trying to slow the interval between looking and making. In the early 1970s, he would stop at random moments and become conscious of what he was seeing, making what he now calls a “screenshot of [his] field of vision.” Later, he walked through New York without a camera, watching visual relationships change as he moved. The point was not simply to find pictures, but to cultivate a way of being in the world. He wanted to capture, he says, “not just the scene, but the act of paying attention, and what it looks like to pay attention.”

It is an idea that lands differently now, when a photograph can be made before the decision to make it has registered. The phone can slip between seeing and thinking; the view camera, by contrast, keeps the apparatus in the body’s awareness. He can stand beside it, register the wind, the light, a shift in someone’s expression. The experience, he says, is deeper – yet he is wary of doctrine. “I’m not writing a prescription,” he says. His hope as a teacher is more modest, but possibly more radical: to help students “see the world with attention.” He extends the thought beyond photography. “I think the world would be a better place if everyone really paid attention.”

Shore does not claim to have discovered a mechanism at Big Bend, only an experience difficult to explain. Perhaps that is the point. The photograph may contain no visible record of the thought that made it, yet something of that thought remains: a trace between the world and the picture, between seeing and photographing, between what can be explained and what can only be noticed. That small gap is where The Mental Image lives. Shore does not close it. He gives it a name.

The Mental Image (2026) by Stephen Shore is published by MACK and available for £20.

article_text:
“ Fjord ,” Cristian Mungiu ’s harrowing and pointedly provocative political drama, has now been open for two weeks, and I have a question about it: Where’s the debate? Where’s the fervor, the fire, the discussion, the arguments, the noise, the sense that a movie like this one matters? Everyone is talking about “You Can See Everything,” parsing the nuances of deceit and what is reality and should we blame it on Billy Evans? (we should not). And that’s a conversation well worth having. But when I saw “Fjord” at the Cannes Film Festival in May, I thought it was a movie that would unleash 1,000 conversations, including some highly incendiary ones, since it’s a film that cuts to the spiritual-ideological heart of so much of what’s happening today.

Related Stories

Paramount Network Orders 13 Original Episodes of Larry the Cable Guy-Hosted Clip Show 'American Mayhem' (EXCLUSIVE)

Instead…crickets. Oh, I see the occasional comment on social media, and I’ve encountered a few passionate and withering denunciations of “Fjord.” But where are the defenders, as well as the fireworks of disagreement?

I think the lack of debate goes back to an experience I had at Cannes that I found at once unsettling and revealing. “Fjord” was quite the conversation piece there — and it won the Palme d’Or, which is one reason it was instantly spoken of as an Oscar contender, not just for best international feature but, potentially, for best picture. I expected “Fjord” to set the media ablaze when it opened. But my experience of how people reacted to it in Cannes is that almost everyone seemed to resist saying out loud what the movie is actually about.

In “Fjord,” Mungiu tells the story of a family — Mihai Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan), who’s Romanian; his wife, Lisbet (Renate Reinsve), who’s Norwegian; and their five children — who have moved from Bucharest to the picturesque Norwegian coastal village that Lisbet is from. The place feels like a tranquil utopia, and for a short while their lives are good. But then, at school, a phys-ed teacher notices that Elia (Vanessa Ceban), the family’s teenage daughter, has a bruise on the back of her shoulder. It’s clear that she has suffered some kind of injury. The question is raised: Was it the result of violence from one of her parents?

The movie doesn’t suggest that it was; the Gheorghius are portrayed as loving and, in their somber evangelical Christian way, rather gentle people. But when the children are questioned, they own up to the fact that their parents have, on occasion, hit them (in the form of a light smack on the butt). Mihai admits to the police that he’s done this, and also that he has, on occasion, slapped their hands (in a way that’s meant to safeguard them — as in, keep your hand away from the stove ). The case becomes an investigation into possible child abuse, and in keeping with the ways of the Norwegian system, the children are immediately taken away and placed in foster care. For how long? An indefinite period. The Gheorghius, it would seem, have done nothing more than, on occasion, lightly smack their children on the rear (something I, as a parent, wouldn’t dream of doing — though it’s not like one or two parents in the Western world haven’t done it). But as they head into a court proceeding, the system looks all but designed to find them guilty. In essence, they face the prospect of having their children taken away, and even the threat of imprisonment, because of a spanking.

At Cannes, I must have had 50 conversations about “Fjord,” and with two exceptions every single person I talked to had the same interpretation of the movie: that it presented “both sides” of the situation, and that it did not take sides. I heard this over and over again. Yet I couldn’t quite believe it. Simply put, that interpretation does not square with the movie I saw. The other thing that was hard to miss in Cannes is that a great many people didn’t care much for “Fjord.” In the two weeks since the movie has opened, however, I’ve spoken to many viewers who have found it powerful. Yet the wrenching drama I experienced onscreen has, for the most part, not been reflected in the critical dialogue about it. Here are a few thoughts on the film, and on the incredibly telling reaction to it.

Why do so many insist that “Fjord” doesn’t choose sides? There are no saints in “Fjord,” and the situation it depicts is not without its ambiguities. The Gheorghius are a family of parochial Christians who oversee their children with a sternly tender and rather old-school command, not allowing them to use tech devices to connect to the outside world. When Elia forms a close bond with her renegade neighbor and classmate, Moora (Henrikke Lund-Olsen), her father glowers in silent disapproval of what may be a romantic attraction; the film looks askance at his homophobic conservatism. As “Fjord” goes on, the film suggests that the hermetic nature of how this family is raising its kids is destined to create problems down the line. In that sense, it’s critical of the family. But it’s not as if any of these sins “balance out” the drastic actions of the Norwegian government. To put it in melodramatic terms, the film has a clearly delineated villain.

That villain is the nanny-state. “Fjord” wears the meditative cloak of an art film, but at heart it’s a political docudrama in the classic tradition of the New Hollywood. The movie is based on an actual case in Norway that it sticks fairly close to, with elements of other European cases mixed in. It’s a film like “Norma Rae” or “Z” or “Erin Brockovich,” in which the protagonists are up against an oppressive system — but in almost every instance of this kind of movie, going back 55 years, the system in question is a right-wing government or a corporate behemoth in league with right-wing power. In “Fjord,” the force that threatens the Gheorghiu family is Norway’s progressive bureaucracy — the Child Services agency, which is so programmed to err on the side of safety that it errs, in this case, on the side of grave inhumanity.

No one watches a muckraking liberal political drama thinking that it gives equal weight to both sides. Well, “Fjord” doesn’t either. But it’s hard to escape the feeling that the reason so many people have rationalized away the film’s moral outlook as a case of both-sides-ism is that they don’t want to acknowledge that a movie that comes from inside the progressive art-film universe — Cristian Mingiu considers himself a liberal — could be critical of the progressive consciousness.

“ Fjord” has been called “a MAGA movie.” Is it? It is not in any way, shape or form. I revere “Fjord” and have no truck with MAGA. At the same time, I’m a staunch progressive who cherishes this movie precisely because I think it’s essential that those of us who carry a progressive sense of justice need to be able to look at our own side and see where it goes astray. “Fjord” is overtly critical of a certain progressive mind-set, one that it sees as rigid and blinkered and even authoritarian. The teachers and school officials who first call the Gheorghius on the carpet, and the Child Services officials who swoop in to investigate and prosecute them, have an infuriatingly smug and blasé manner. They’re talking about taking people’s children away, and they sound like they’re discussing tax law. They know that they have the weight of the system behind then, but what they also have is the weight of an ideology, one that has taken the unassailable issue of children’s well-being and placed it on a pedestal of absolutism.

The movie is about something bigger than “the system in Norway. ” Just as “Norma Rae” was about something bigger than the exploitation of cotton-mill workers in North Carolina, “Fjord,” while it’s set with pinpoint precision in a particular time and place, uses the specificity of that setting to make a statement about a more widespread ideological belief system. And that state of mind is: The Child Services officials believe they have the right to take the Georghius’ children away. Legally (in Norway), they do, but what that reflects is a belief in a state authority that is all-powerful — an ironic position coming from those who’ve pledged to protect the powerless from the powerful.

“ Fjord” is an outcry against anti-Christian prejudice. But if that’s the only message you take from it… The movie sets up a spiritual battle between the New Europe progressives and the Old Europe Christians. The Norwegian officials are so suspect of the Georghius’ evangelical roots and practices that their attitude is portrayed — quite rightly — as bigotry. “Am I on trial for my beliefs?” asks Mihai from the witness stand. To a certain degree, he is. But only to a degree. More to the point: If that’s the only message you take away from “Fjord” — that the last thing a government that thinks of itself as enlightened should be doing is clamping down on a family of traditional Christians for their beliefs — then you’ve missed the forest for the trees. For that’s a theme you could get from almost any liberal message movie: Don’t be prejudiced. But that’s not the ultimate message of “Fjord.” The ultimate message of “Fjord” is: Beware a system so convinced of its own virtue that it’s willing to destroy what it’s pretending to save.

Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink: The Art of Wesley Tongson / Jul 15 – Oct 11, 2026 / Piano Recital : Sunday, Oct 11, 4pm – 5pm / Miller Theater, The Imagined Pianist: Christina Petrowska Quilico /

Chantal Miller Gallery Asia Society Hong Kong Center 9 Justice Drive Admiralty Tuesday – Sunday, 11am – 6pm +852 2103 9511

asiasociety.org

Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink: The Art of Wesley Tongson , the final installation of Asia Society Hong Kong Center’s Celebration of Ink exhibition series, runs through 11 October at ASHK’s Chantal Miller Gallery.

Representing the first major institutional exhibition of Wesley Tongson (Tang Jiawei 唐家偉, 1957–2012) in his home city in over a decade, the show highlights his mastery of classical subjects and the innovative “ink play” techniques through which he transformed daily struggles into rich artistic visions of landscapes, expressive finger-painting, and transcendent splashed ink works.

Upcoming programs include a lecture on post-’80s Hong Kong ink painting by academic experts from the Greater Bay Area (late September), and a performance of Alice Ping Yi Ho’s Pictures from an Imagined Exhibition , inspired by Tongson’s dynamic works, performed by celebrated Canadian pianist Christina Petrowska Quilico (October 11). Complimentary guided tours in English and Cantonese are offered weekly.

The exhibition is co-curated by Yi Yi Mon (Rosaline) Kyo and Julia M. White, with support provided by the Asia Society Hong Kong Center Gallery & Exhibitions Team.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : LA-based producer-financier Christa Campbell has launched film, TV and media company XTA Media , which has seed funding from London and Denmark-based private investment firm Three Thousand Capital.

Campbell’s credits as a producer and exec producer include Hellboy , Rambo: Last Blood , The Iceman , Leatherface , The Hitman’s Bodyguard , The Hitman’s Wife’s Bodyguard , Texas Chainsaw 3D , Tesla , Red Sonja , and the Oscar-nominated documentary Winter on Fire: Ukraine’s Fight for Freedom .

Until recently the former actress ran Campbell Grobman Films with Lati Grobman.

Watch on Deadline

'Avengers: Doomsday' World Series Sneak Peek Sees Mister Fantastic Throw Out First Pitch

According to Campbell, the new company comes with a sizeable capital injection and will acquire IP, develop original and adapted material, finance productions, and produce content for film, TV and other media platforms.

Campbell’s upcoming projects include the new John Rambo film and the KISS biopic , Shout It Out Loud , set up at Lionsgate.

“I started XTA Media to build a company that owns its stories from the first idea to the final cut,” said Campbell. “Having this level of capital in place from day one lets us go after the projects we believe in, whether they’re big franchises or original voices, on our own terms. Three Thousand Capital understands both the creative and business sides of this industry, and they’re the right partner to build with.”

Since 2012, Three Thousand Capital has completed more than 100 direct private investments in entertainment, music, the platform economy and big tech. Early stage investments have included Uber, Airbnb, Shazam, SoundCloud, Duolingo, Spotify and X (Twitter). The firm is also developing a feature film in Scandinavia, slated for theatrical release in 2027.

“Christa has a rare track record of turning major IP into global hits while also championing films that matter, like Winter on Fire ,” said Michael Peen of Three Thousand Capital. “We’ve spent more than a decade backing founders who reshape their industries, and XTA Media is exactly that kind of opportunity. We’re very excited about this new venture and proud to be a founding partner.”

La tercera temporada de El Señor de los Anillos: Los Anillos de Poder , Blade Runner 2099 y la película Madden se destacan entre los principales lanzamientos del mes.

Prime Video renueva su catálogo en noviembre de 2026 con una selección de películas, series y propuestas de entretenimiento para todos los gustos. Entre los lanzamientos más destacados se encuentran la tercera temporada de El Señor de los Anillos: Los Anillos de Poder , la esperada serie Blade Runner 2099 y Madden , una película inspirada en la vida de una de las figuras más importantes del fútbol americano. Además, la plataforma sumará nuevas producciones de comedia, romance y acción, junto con encuentros de la temporada 2026-2027 de la NBA.

La Mangosta – 4 de noviembre

Ryan “Fang” Flanagan (Liam Neeson), un veterano de guerra acusado injustamente de un crimen, huye de la policía a bordo de un Mustang Shelby Cobra GT 65. Sin nada que perder, protagoniza una intensa persecución por las carreteras del país.

Campus Drivers – 6 de noviembre

Lois llega a la universidad con un futuro prometedor, pero una decepción amorosa la lleva a convivir con Lane, un joven popular que evita los compromisos y creador de Campus Drivers, la app más popular del campus. Entre sus diferencias surge una atracción inesperada que pondrá a prueba sus sentimientos y despertará heridas del pasado.

El Señor de los Anillos: Los Anillos de Poder – 11 de noviembre

La temporada 3 tiene lugar en el apogeo de la Guerra de los Elfos y Sauron, mientras el Señor Oscuro busca forjar el Anillo Único que le dará la ventaja que necesita para ganar la guerra, atar a todos los pueblos a su voluntad y al fin gobernar toda la Tierra Media.

Madden – 18 de noviembre

Inspirada en la vida de John Madden, la película narra su trayectoria junto a Al Davis, desde su triunfo con los Raiders en el Super Bowl hasta convertirse en una de las voces más reconocidas del fútbol americano y crear el exitoso videojuego Madden NFL.

article_text:
The Lego Group has appointed its first head of celebrity talent and brand first partnerships.

Kelsey Gray Sherman has joined the company in the Hollywood whisperer role, which is part of the Entertainment, Partnerships & Content division. The new position “reflects the company’s growing focus on expanding the Lego brand’s presence across entertainment and culture,” according to a press release. Sherman will shape the toy and media company’s approach to celebrity talent, identifying and building relationships with entertainers and brands in ways that go beyond traditional licensing and product collaborations.

Related Stories

Kevin Delaney Takes Role as NBC News' Head of Digital Content and Subscription

Sherman, who comes to Lego from WME, where she served as the vice president of the Entertainment Marketing & Advisory group, will be based in Los Angeles. She will report directly to Jill Wilfert, Lego’s senior vice president of Entertainment, Partnerships & Content, and will serve as a member of the division’s leadership team.

“Kelsey brings deep relationships across the talent and entertainment communities, along with a strong understanding of the Lego brand,” said Wilfert. “She knows how to bring together the right talent, partners and ideas in ways that feel fresh and authentic, and her experience and instincts will be invaluable as we continue to grow our work in entertainment and culture.”

Sherman added, “Having worked closely with the Lego Group for many years, I’ve seen first-hand its unique ability to bring together entertainment, experiences and culture. I’m excited to build on that strength through ambitious, distinctive partnerships with exceptional talent and brands. Together, we can create new ways to inspire creativity and play and connect with audiences around the world.”

Lego has built a large presence in the entertainment industry and cultural zeitgeist, with partnerships that date back decades. The company’s collaboration with the “Star Wars” franchise, for example, includes toy sets, television projects and a popular video game. The flagship Lego movies are considered big successes, and the company even partnered with Pharrell Williams in 2024 to create a biopic animated entirely with Lego bricks.

article_text:
T his Margate shop is now an ice-cream parlour, but back in 2014 it was a vintage clothes store. Mark McEvoy, who had relocated from London the previous year with his partner and baby daughter, approached the young woman to ask permission to take this shot.

“I remember it being a very cold October day, so I was surprised she was barelegged and barefoot,” he says. “My guess is that she was working in the shop, or maybe a friend of someone working there. The fur coat may even have been for sale inside, just something she put on to keep warm during a cigarette break.”

McEvoy didn’t notice the blond-haired, barelegged mannequin in the window until he stepped back. “A gust of wind blowing back her hair and her pose added something special,” he notes.

In more recent years, McEvoy has been scanning and collating his 40-year archive of photographs, and reflecting on his work across various devices and formats; a range of iPhone models but also analogue cameras, both 35mm and medium format. “I am a bit of a purist, inspired by the documentary tradition of cropping in the frame when you take the photo. So, rather than say to myself, ‘I can crop that out in post’, I’ll move physically closer to the subject instead,” McEvoy says.

It’s an approach he would recommend to any aspiring photographer. “These days, with AI and advanced editing software, it’s too easy to manipulate a photo, and the line between fact and fiction becomes more and more blurred.”

article_text:
Sur son compte Instagram , Zhenya publie des collages empreints d’une sombre poésie. Une collection de « résidus visuels » qui convoque les mystères de son monde intérieur.

Dans un espace monochrome, une pupille rouge déchire l’obscurité. Elle suit du regard le corps tout aussi écarlate d’une araignée. Plus loin, un poème s’efface dans un pli de page, son sens noyé par les vagues qui l’entourent. Et puis, il y a ces silhouettes étranges qui errent d’une publication à l’autre, ces fleurs colorées en négatif qui grimpent le long de visual residue, compte Instagram et journal illustré de Zhenya, alias @unknwnrt.

Originaire de Saint-Pétersbourg, c’est en 2007 qu’elle se lance dans le collage, lorsqu’un ami à elle lui fait découvrir Photoshop. Une expérience qu’elle qualifie de « non linéaire ». « Avec des périodes où je tombe en désamour de cette pratique. Et pourtant, j’y reviens toujours d’une manière ou d’une autre », ajoute-t-elle . Une façon pour elle de déposer des impressions, des atmosphères sur ses créations, de se détendre quelques heures, libérée des pressions du quotidien en s’échappant dans les univers qu’elle compose.

Le familier devenu liminal

Adepte du numérique, Zhenya conçoit ses collages en multipliant les logiciels, plug-ins et codes pour superposer les couches, dénicher de nouvelles textures et s’arrêter sur ce qui pique son intérêt. « Ce qui me plaît surtout, c’est de trouver quelque chose qui existe déjà et de le retirer de son contexte d’origine pour le transformer en lui donnant une relation différente à son environnement » , explique-t-elle. De ses expérimentations émergent des figures étranges, fragments parfois sombres et mystérieux qui reviennent hanter ses images, d’une réalisation à l’autre. Jouant avec la distorsion, elle laisse apparaître des yeux isolés de leurs corps, des branches mortes et fleurs arrachées à leur tige, des mains gracieuses et des arches gothiques perdues dans un brouillard noir fait de grain et de contrastes prononcés. « J’aime particulièrement lorsque le familier devient liminal, comme s’il n’appartenait pas vraiment à ce monde », explique-t-elle.

Des architectures émotionnelles

Une démarche qu’elle juge « méditative ». Ne souhaitant pas produire un art qui entendrait dénoncer quelque chose, Zhenya perçoit davantage son compte Instagram comme un espace de stockage de ses expérimentations plutôt qu’une galerie numérique. Pour elle, tout l’intérêt de ses compositions réside dans leur développement. « C’est le processus de création qui me fascine, je ne suis pas particulièrement attachée à mes collages, c’est comme si une fois finis, ils cessaient de remplir leur fonction », précise-t-elle. Qualifiant ses œuvres « d’architectures émotionnelles », elle tisse des ponts de son esprit à ses fichiers – laissant ceux-ci devenir les réceptacles de sensations, de pensées dont elle se déleste. Des ruminations nourries par « une nostalgie constante de choses qui ne se sont pas produites et ne se produiront probablement jamais », un monologue intérieur façonné par un goût prononcé pour la musique et un attrait pour la nature. Et de cet imaginaire naît un univers fait de brumes et d’éclats, d’où surgissent formes spectrales et envolées poétiques – protagonistes que Zhenya préfère voir évoluer au bon vouloir des regardeur·ses.

Intime

article_text:
Erinnerungen an Rudi Fuchs, Anselm Kiefer über die AfD und Museen als Gegenpol zu KI-Schrott: Das ist unsere Presseschau am Mittwoch

Rechtsruck in Deutschland

Der Künstler Anselm Kiefer hat sich zu den Wahlerfolgen der AfD geäußert . Nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg seien rechtsextreme Tendenzen in der Gesellschaft verdeckt und verdrängt worden, sagte der 81-Jährige der "Stuttgarter Zeitung" . Aber sie seien immer da gewesen. Er habe schon früh gesagt, dass der Sumpf nicht ausgetrocknet sei. "Diese faschistischen Züge verschwinden nicht einfach." Man müsse nun dagegen kämpfen. Eine neue Ausstellung mit mehr als 90 meist großformatigen Werken von Kiefer ist seit Mitte Oktober in der Kunsthalle Würth in Schwäbisch Hall zu sehen.

Nachruf

Bei "ArtNews" erinnert Anne Doran an den verstorbenen Kurator und Museumsdirektor Rudi Fuchs , der in Deutschland vor allem als Leiter der Documenta 7 bekannt ist. Die Autorin schreibt, dass der Niederländer oft als zu konservativ und zu westlich orientiert kritisiert wurde. Aber er habe es verstanden, sein Publikum zu überraschen. "Im Stedelijk Museum war Fuchs – der bekanntlich keine Wandbeschriftungen mochte – für seine impressionistische Kuration bekannt, die er mit dem Komponieren von Musik oder dem Schreiben eines Theaterstücks verglich", schreibt Doran. "Eine Serie mit dem Titel 'Couplets' beispielsweise brachte historische Werke aus der Sammlung des Museums mit Arbeiten zeitgenössischer Künstler wie Donald Judd, Jannis Kounellis und Karel Appel zusammen. Er lud auch Außenstehende ein, darunter im Jahr 2000 Königin Beatrix, Ausstellungen zu kuratieren." Der Artikel zitiert auch den aktuellen Stedelijk-Direktor Rein Wolfs: "Rudi hat wesentlich zum Verständnis von Kunst beigetragen; alles, was er tat, regte dazu an, wirklich hinzuschauen." Den Monopol-Nachruf auf Rudi Fuchs lesen Sie hier.

Surrealismus

Wie Dorothea Tanning oder Meret Oppenheim war, wie Hans-Joachim Müller in der "Welt" etwas giftig schreibt, Leonor Fini (1907–1996) "großzügig respektiertes Mitglied im Gral der Surrealisten". Da sie weder zum "Volksheldentum eines Salvador Dalí" aufsteigen konnte noch den Ruhm des "Ober-Dada Max Ernst" erlangen konnte – sie war ja eine Frau –, wundert es auch Müller kaum, dass Fini erst 30 Jahre nach ihrem Tod mit einer angemessenen Retrospektive gewürdigt wird. Die Schau "Leonor Fini" in der Frankfurter Schirn Kunsthalle läuft bis 21. Februar und entfaltet mit über 100 Werken, darunter Gemälde, Zeichnungen, Fotografien und Objekte, das Œuvre der italienischen Künstlerin. Restlos begeistert ist Müller von der Wiederentdeckung aber nicht. "Wie soll man das Werk beschreiben? Soll man sagen: ein bisschen brav, artig, stachellos, nicht wirklich tiefgründig?", schreibt der Rezensent. "Es hat auch etwas Versöhnliches, wie die Malerin ihre Bühnen mit gut verträglichen Bizarrerien bevölkert, wie da und dort ein Maskengesicht aus dem Farbfond schimmert und es aufs Ganze betrachtet auch nicht viel anders zugeht als in einer zeitgemäßeren Variante der Walpurgisnacht." Müllers These: Die Bilder bergen "ein Drama, das tunlichst versteckt bleiben will. Vielleicht decken sie die kämpferische Lebensrolle, erzählen von nichts anderem als vom femininen Stolz, von der überlegenen Selbstbehauptung inmitten einer maskulinen Kultur, vom giftigen Stachel des Skorpions, den drohend vorzuhalten ungleich sinnvoller erscheint, als neue Kunstrevolutionen anzuzetteln." Kurzum: Trotz Leonor Finis verdientem Platz in der Kunstgeschichte, sogar ihrem "Genie, mit dem sie die Tradition der figürlichen Malerei fortsetzt" – "zu den Pionierinnen hat sie nicht gehört. Hat sie, die nur ihre eigenen Maßstäbe kannte, gar nicht gehören wollen", schließt Hans-Joachim Müller.

Museen

Im "New Yorker" macht sich Rebecca Mead für Museen als Gegenpol zu KI-Schrott stark. Als Beispiel zieht sie das Victoria and Albert Museum heran, das in London gleich zwei neue Standorte eröffnet hat: ein Schaulager und das V&A East. In Zeiten von KI-generiertem Einheitsbrei machten die beiden neuen Häuser lebendige Werbung für menschliches kreatives Schaffen und Begegnungen im "echten" Leben. Ein Interview mit dem V&A-East-Direktor Gus Casely-Hayford lesen Sie hier .

Geburtstagsgrüße

Sie besitzen keinen Hals, nur wenig Brust und Bauch, und Kopf und Füße scheinen ineinander überzugehen: Die "Kopffüßler" sind das berühmteste Motiv des Künstlers Horst Antes und dominieren entsprechend auch die Hommage, die die "FAZ" dem Heppenheimer zum 90. Geburtstag schenkt. Antes’ ikonische Wesen gehörten "spätestens seit der allabendlichen Präsenz in den bundesrepublikanischen Nachrichten vom Bonner Rheinufer unauslöschlich zum vertrauten Bildhaushalt der deutschen Boomer und der Generation Golf", schreibt Stefan Trinks. "Seit 1962 gibt es sie gemalt und skulptiert, so holzschnittartig derb und plakativ farbig wie in Bewegung gesetzte Pop-Art." Geprägt wurde Antes unter anderem von seinem Lehrer HAP Grieshaber und dessen Farbholzschnitten. Seine Kunst verbinde Einflüsse aus Psychologie, Anthropologie und verschiedenen historischen Kulturen, etwa durch die Auseinandersetzung mit mittelalterlichen Darstellungen und indigenen Figuren. Die weite Verbreitung seiner Werke zeigt seinen großen Erfolg, führt laut Trinks jedoch auch dazu, dass seine Figuren allgegenwärtig erscheinen.

article_text:
Marchers from the first demonstrations for homosexual rights, nurses of the AIDS years, performers of the night: across 250 portraits gathered at the National Portrait Gallery, Tim Walker ennobles the heralds of his community.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Tim Walker.

Tim Walker came into the world on November 27, 1970, in England. That same day, on Highbury Fields, Britons marched for homosexual rights for the first time. Did this calendrical coincidence seal a destiny? Whatever the answer, the photographer took up with the queer community and its allies, and now exhibits 250 previously unseen portraits of them. “Fairyland is me saying you are not alone,” says Tim Walker.

Lace ruffs and gilded frames open the show: the trailblazers of the 1970s and 1980s pose in the finery of Tudor portraits painted by Hans Holbein the Younger, portraitist to Henry VIII, and Nicholas Hilliard, miniaturist to Elizabeth I. Tim Walker thus raises the founders of the Gay Liberation Front and Stonewall, Olivette Cole-Wilson and Lisa Power among them, into his own “queeristocracy.” Shona Heath, an Oscar winner for the sets of Poor Things , designed the exhibition. All of it unfolds along “a journey that begins with protest and outrage and ends with joy,” says curator Susanna Brown.

On the day of the shoot, each sitter arrives bearing a cherished object. Filmmaker Isaac Julien cradles a conch shell, a motif from his film Looking for Langston (1989); Welsh actress Jill Nalder, who inspired the character of Jill in It’s a Sin , holds in her open palm a photograph of actor Dursley McLinden, lost to AIDS in 1995. Writer Shon Faye, poet Kae Tempest and Lady Phyll, cofounder of UK Black Pride, pose against “deceivingly simple” white backgrounds inherited from Richard Avedon, the American master of the portrait whom Tim Walker assisted in the 1990s. Ian McKellen, for his part, spells the word Love with his fingers.

An entire room honors those who faced down the AIDS epidemic of the 1980s. Portraits of the nurses and doctors who developed effective treatments hang beside Marc Almond, voice of the synth-pop duo Soft Cell, Holly Johnson, singer of the Liverpool band Frankie Goes to Hollywood and Jimmy Somerville, whose falsetto carried Bronski Beat. “The brilliance of their music boomed despite the fear of mortality and discrimination. I wanted to bring that disco to the ward,” says Tim Walker. At the center, the Rebel Dykes, a lesbian collective out of post-punk London, pose on a grand scale, in the vein of the Zurich biker gangs photographed by Swiss photographer Karlheinz Weinberger.

Fashion, makeup and performance reign over the second half of the exhibition. French couturier Jean Paul Gaultier shares the walls with David Hoyle, a figure of English avant-garde cabaret, and Paul O’Grady, the comedian who died in 2023, unforgettable as Lily Savage, whom Tim Walker crowns a Glitter Queen beside comedian Julian Clary, amid clouds and bubbles. Victoria Siddall, director of the National Portrait Gallery, salutes these “lavish, fantastical scenes.” The last room gives way to the flesh, where eroticism reworks fairy tales and nursery rhymes. Tim Walker holds that voluptuousness, and the humor that rides with it, to be “the very heart of what we’re talking about when we talk about Queerness. A place where you can desire and be desired. A place where you can be whoever you want to be.”

“Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends” runs at the National Portrait Gallery, London, through February 7, 2027.

The exhibition catalogue, Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends , is published by National Portrait Gallery Publications (320 pages, £35).

Sam Fleischner is a filmmaker and co-founder and Artistic Director of the Rockaway Film Festival, where he leads the design and construction of its cinema spaces. His films include “Stand Clear of the Closing Doors,” “Wah Do Dem,” “Below the Brain,” and “Donald Cried.” His most recent film, “Jetty” (2025), examines the reconstruction of Rockaway’s coastline and the human impulse to out-engineer nature.

It’s always tragic when a cinema goes dark. With the recent news of the Kips Bay AMC shuttering, the term “cinema desert” has resurfaced. It’s a relative term, though, especially in New York City, one of the greatest cinema cities in the world, with incredible theaters, programming, and devoted audiences. But the real cinema deserts of NYC exist farther out, in places like the Rockaways.

Over the course of the 20th century, the Rockaways had nine movie theaters: movie palaces in Far Rockaway, a cinema built over the water on the Arverne pier, and neighborhood theaters like the Surfside Twin, the last to close in 1996. Since then, getting to the movies has generally meant traveling for more than an hour each way for the 125,000 full-time residents of the peninsula.

This was the driving force behind the Rockaway Film Festival , which launched in 2018. We wanted to bring cinema back to a place that had lost it, and a festival was a low-stakes experiment to test the waters. People showed up. For the past six years, we have operated a temporary, community-built, open-air theater called Arverne Cinema.

The organization has become more than a film festival, and more than a series of movie screenings. The experience extends before and after the film and encompasses everything from the approach to the venue, to the food and drinks served, to music and dancing, and, most fundamentally, the exchange between artists and audience. Most of what we have built has been ephemeral, but our audience has endured, and that has kept us devoted to this work.

Rockaway itself is an unusually cinematic place, with its open sky and quixotic light. Dolphins, surfers, and cargo ships move across the horizon of the Atlantic. Across Jamaica Bay, you can see the Manhattan skyline and the constant movement of planes coming in and out of JFK. The dense housing reflects the backgrounds and histories of people who have arrived from all over the world, by choice or by circumstance, and the mixture has produced a culture all its own.

While it’s impossible to satisfy everyone’s cinematic tastes, curating for such a diverse audience presents a particular challenge. Of course, many residents would love to see the latest franchise movie on the biggest IMAX screen. But it’s worth asking what we miss when that becomes the default. The industry has engineered a system in which the stories are the same, the stars are the same, and the formulas are the same. We call this entertainment, but it is also an enormous machine for manufacturing sameness, with profit as its organizing principle. And the many multiplex cinemas built to accommodate that output are also generic, and often they’re the ones that have been closing, one after another.

In a society ruled by capitalism, there is an assumption that everything be done for profit, and if that’s not the mission, it falls into a special category all its own: nonprofit – everyone run before they’re asked to donate! But aren’t some of the most valuable things in life – including art and culture – valuable precisely because they are not driven by profit? Perhaps their value lies in their resistance to that logic, and to the monoculture it produces. I’m not sure I have anything new to add to the age-old debate between art and commerce, but it’s impossible to ignore when thinking about the future of cinema. The idea that some things are worth doing simply because they enrich our lives, rather than because they generate a return, feels increasingly fragile.

Cinema has always been more than either art or entertainment. It is a gathering place for people to experience something collectively, apart from the arena or the cathedral. In its short lifespan, cinema has evolved from a facsimile of live theater, to sound pictures, added color, new aspect ratios, 3D, IMAX, 4DX, and on and on. There is always a new spectacle, a new gimmick to lure people into a theater and justify the cost of a ticket. But what about the simple draw of a shared experience that brings us back to something as primal as storytelling around a fire?

And what about films not designed around formulas, stars, spectacle, awards and profit? What about the strange, transcendent experiences that only fully reveal themselves when encountered collectively, in a room, over time? How do we preserve and present these works as events, much as theater has historically existed as a live art form?

When we make the effort to go out, we want it to be worthwhile, and the evidence is already here. Over the past decade or more, New York City moviegoers have shown a real appetite for this kind of experience. Repertory screenings on 35mm film, artist presentations at microcinemas, and other special programs continue to draw full audiences. People will show up to watch something they’ve never heard of simply because someone they trust has built an experience around it.

This feels especially important now, as people grow more isolated, and speaks to some of our most basic needs as a species. Since the pandemic, a loneliness epidemic has continued to spread, while we spend more of our lives alone with personalized feeds of imagery and information. As we gravitate toward convenience, something essential is lost when experience becomes individualized. A community is a kind of cultural petri dish: a physical environment where ideas collide, artists experiment, and unexpected things can happen. Culture emerges from proximity, friction, and coincidence. This is why we need not only to create more cinemas, but to rethink their design and function so they can be sustainable.

As we look for space and begin to fundraise for a permanent home for cinema in Rockaway, there are many considerations. The program will encompass everything from blockbusters to obscure documentaries, silent classics with live accompaniment, films from around the world, expanded cinema, and everything in between film and performance. The space must be flexible: optimized for film but able to transform for other uses like dancing, concert, puppet theater, private event space, or film production location. A kitchen will serve delicious food and drinks, with plenty of comfortable space for people to sit, talk, and gather before and after events.

There are examples of this model all over the world, but we need more of them here in the United States, and I wish for each one to be as unique as the community it serves. As we establish our own version in Rockaway, I hope it can serve as a useful model and contribute to a broader network of small, independent cinemas capable of doing what a centralized commercial distribution system cannot. By prioritizing cooperation over competition, we can use our interconnected world to share infrastructure, knowledge, and resources while providing meaningful, sustained support for artists and filmmakers.

Cinemas are a public good, strengthening communities, supporting local economies, and cultivating the next generation of storytellers and audiences. They invite us to put down our devices, pay attention, and experience new perspectives. Cinema was always a technology for capturing the human experience and bringing us together in the dark to imagine other worlds. Perhaps its future depends on remembering why it mattered in the first place. Where will we gather? How will we connect in real life? If cinema is to survive, we must protect spaces for collective imagination – and recognize that building them and maintaining them is, above all, a human endeavor.
excerpt_original: The co-founder of the Rockaway Film Festival on developing a new model for community cinema.

article_text:
Pipo Nguyen-duy , a professor at Ohio’s Oberlin College and Conservatory and a recipient of the Guggenheim Fellowship in photography, was found dead at 64 in an off-campus home on Wednesday.

ABC News reports that Nguyen-duy’s son, Daniel Jones (formerly known as Asia Nguyen-duy), has been charged in connection with a double homicide for the murder of his father and stepmother, Tran Thi Phong. Nguyen-duy and Phong were found fatally shot by local police.

“The male victim was discovered on the first floor of the residence, and the female victim was discovered on the second floor. Both victims suffered from multiple gunshot wounds,” police said in a statement on Thursday. The victims’ bodies were discovered on Wednesday.

Jones appeared in court on Thursday afternoon in handcuffs and ankle shackles. He was ordered to be held in jail, and a bail was set at $3 million. Jones was arrested on Wednesday without incident after an Oberlin resident called police to report a “wet disheveled man” at her front door. About 90 minutes before the bodies were found, police officers were called to an Oberlin College campus parking lot to support firefighters extinguishing a fire in a vehicle that was registered to Jones.

In court, prosecutor Zachary Simonoff said that Jones asked the resident to record a video of him to post online. “He told her that he did not want the police involved. In the video, he identifies himself as Asia Nguyen-duy, says he’s escaping a cult. He also says, ‘Everything I did was on my own accord and I take full responsibility,’” said Simonoff in court. “Officers went there and found two people dead apparently from gunshot wounds with blood throughout the house.” In court, Simonoff said that Jones told officers that he “killed his family” when they first spoke to him and gave the officers his father’s address.

Simonoff added that police have contacted Jones’s mother in Oregon. She told them that her son is psychotic and needs medication. A motive for the shooting remains under investigation.

The weapon allegedly used in the shooting has not been found, according to the prosecutor.

Pipo Nguyen-duy had been a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College since 1998. “Tragedies such as this one intrude upon our lives in jarring ways. I am simply overwhelmed with sadness, and I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community,” said Oberlin College President Carmen Twillie Ambar in a statement on Wednesday addressed to students and colleagues. “Pipo was beloved. During his years at Oberlin, he touched all of us through his passion for photography. Our community will be hurting for a very long time, and when the shock of this news subsides, we will all need to process our grief. This process will sometimes be together and sometimes alone, but we will need to take the time to do so.”

Nguyen-duy had immigrated from Vietnam in 1975 as a political refugee and went on to become an internationally exhibited visual artist. He took up photography in his late 20s and pursued it academically, receiving his MA and MFA from the University of New Mexico at Albuquerque. “In his wide-ranging body of work, Nguyen-duy considered immigration and emigration, intimacy, abandonment and decay, cultural assimilation, and the cost of war,” said a tribute post from the Guggenheim Foundation on Instagram. “And he touched people all over the world with his probing, compassionate work.”

In 2023, Nguyen-duy participated in the 15th Sharjah Biennial , exhibiting photographs of schoolchildren playing in what looks like the Vietnam countryside, with some napping on felled trees while others have assault rifles tucked under their arms.
excerpt_original: Nguyen-duy was an internationally exhibited visual artist and recipient of the Guggenheim Fellowship in photography.

article_text:
The JustWatch Group, known for its guide to streaming , is officially in the programming game after Tuesday’s launch of multi-dimensional platform JustWatch TV.

The Berlin-based company, which was founded in 2014, said the new service will offer free and ad-supported video on demand and transactional titles from 30 initial partners from the U.S. and other countries. A premium ad-free tier will be available for $3.99 a month.

Plans for the service were revealed last month.

JustWatch TV is launching in the U.S., Canada, the UK, Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Australia and New Zealand. It is available within the JustWatch apps and website, which has 50 million users.

Watch on Deadline

Peter Rice Will Blend "Art And Commerce" In Heading Content For Netflix, Ted Sarandos Says

Netflix Stock Falls Despite Solid Q3 Results On Lowered Advertising Guidance, Disappointing Revenue Outlook

Initial content partners include Cineverse in the US, Leonine Studios in Germany, SND in France, and Altitude in the UK & Ireland. They join previously announced suppliers Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street and Vortex Media.

“The launch of JustWatch TV marks the most important new development in our company’s twelve-year history, and it’s only the start,” says David Croyé, Founder and CEO of the JustWatch Group. “We called our company JustWatch because we wanted to make it easier for people to find and ‘just watch’ the movies and shows they love. From the beginning, our vision was to create a single platform that directs fans to all of their entertainment options in one place. JustWatch TV will help fill in the gaps and will make it easier for the massive JustWatch audience to discover and watch great movies and series, including those hard-to-find titles, right from the app itself.” The JustWatch Group has 200-plus employees spread across its Berlin-based headquarters and offices in L.A., London, Paris, Rome, Madrid, Munich, Dubai, and Sydney.

解説・あらすじ

沖縄の島々に暮らす人たちの声から、沖縄と日本の関係を見つめ直したドキュメンタリー。 豊かな自然と温暖な気候に恵まれ、琉球王国時代から受け継がれてきた独自の文化・風習をもつ沖縄の島々。その一方で、戦争では20万人以上が犠牲となり、戦後も日本国内における米軍基地の約7割がこの地に集まり、県民所得は全国最下位で3人に1人の子どもが貧困状態にある。戦後81年、本土復帰54年を経た現在、沖縄では何が起こり、そこに暮らす人々は何を見つめ、どのような問題と向き合っているのか。10代から80代までの市井の人々の語りの集積から、沖縄の実像を重層的に浮かび上がらせていく。 監督は、大袈裟太郎という芸名でも知られるジャーナリストでラッパーの猪股東吾。東京から沖縄に移住して取材を続けるなかで、沖縄が抱えるさまざまな問題の根幹に「本土」側の無関心と構造的差別があることを実感した猪股監督が、「やまとんちゅ（本土出身者）」という立場から初メガホンをとり、4年の歳月をかけて完成させた。

article_text:
“ Green Room ” writer and director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to late actor Patrick Stewart , who starred in the film and whom he credits with saving the day when they were “close to shutting down,” during a 10th-anniversary screening of the 2015 film in Los Angeles on Friday. Stewart died one day earlier, on Thursday, at 86.

“Who’s sad as fuck we lost Patrick Stewart yesterday? Me,” said Saulnier during his introduction to the movie. “I came here to shamelessly promote Slayground, but instead, I’m just gonna celebrate Patrick Stewart. He had no business doing this movie. He had plenty of opportunities otherwise.” His star power revitalized the production when it was “at the point of no return,” and no one had been cast as Darcy Banker, the skinhead leader Stewart ultimately played. “We’re fucked, and we were close to shutting down,” he said.

Netflix Content Chief Bela Bajaria on Overseeing Global Storytelling: 'My Super Power Is I Hire Really Great People and I Let Them Do Their Job'

Then, “Patrick Stewart, out of the blue, sort of expressed interest in the project,” said Saulnier. “And in a whirlwind about a week later, I was on the phone with him. I left the stage, ‘Maybe we’re gonna have to break down the sets and shut the whole movie down.’

He continued: “Instead, this dude came out of nowhere, from way above our sort of zone, and just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us, and said yes. And the movie was instantly greenlit; we moved forward. And I thank him for just taking that leap and making ‘Green Room’ a thing.”

Saulnier remembered the actor as a “fucking sweetheart, true gentleman, a kind leader to our whole cast,” and recounted his idea to add “a little something” to one scene: “I was like, ‘What is it, Patrick?’ He’s like, ‘Well, during this one part of the scene, when the camera’s coming through there, I’d like to say, “Fuck!” And I was like, ‘And?’ ‘Just fuck.’ Permission granted, sir,” Saulnier recounted. “And I just knew that he was completely aligned with the film, its aesthetic, its intentions and with me as a filmmaker, and it was just this lovely, lovely thing.”

Stewart died after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement on his Instagram account. He was best known for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on “ Star Trek: The Next Generation ” and as Professor Charles Xavier in the “ X-Men ” films, among many other film and TV credits.

article_text:
Colin From Accounts actor Patrick Brammall has changed speeds with his latest series, Apple TV mystery drama Last Seen .

The drama, which rolled out its final episode on October 7 to good reviews, came after Brammall and his on-screen partner and real-life wife Harriet Dyer brought their much-loved Australian comedy Colin From Accounts to a close after three seasons.

Brammall said switching to a dramatic role of a father desperately searching for his-long lost daughter was “a bit scary and attractive at the same time,” as he paid tribute to Apple pushing into Australian originals for the first time and director Christian Schwochow, known for work on the likes of The Crown and feature film Munich ’38 .

Related Stories

Bill Nighy Joins Alfonso Cuarón's Apple TV Horror Thriller Series 'Ascension'

'Wentworth: Halfway Home': Grace Chow & Nadine Garner Among 9 Joining Cast; Watch Trailer

“Apple has the resources, so we had time to shoot,” he added. “We were not struggling to shoot nine or 12 minutes a day, or constantly facing the light. We had a 100-day shoot, and you can see it. The production value is there. It looks fantastic.”

Watch on Deadline

He also reflected on the end of Colin , which was ordered out of Australia at the ABC and played in the U.S. on Paramount+ and in the UK on the BBC. “I am starting to feel the legacy of it,” said the writer and actor, while also explaining on the decision to stop after three seasons.

He also revealed the much-loved, feel-good show was almost not centered on a mismatched couple attempting to nurse an injured dog back to health. Instead, Brammall and Dyer came close to substituting Colin with an elderly lady, before reverting to their original premise. “We talked about making a statement about how we treat older people,” he said.

Elsewhere in the interview, Brammall spoke about his role as Andy’s (Anne Hathaway) love interest Peter in The Devil Wears Prada 2 . “Even though it was a massive movie, the set was often very relaxed,” he said. “There were a couple of days when people gathered in the street to watch, which was strange.”

Deadline spoke to Brammall during a recent trip to London.

DEADLINE: The success of Colin will have opened up new avenues for you and Harriet. Last Seen like Colin is about family, although in a completely different way. What attracted you to it?

Patrick Brammall: The first thing I knew was that it was a big Apple show and their first major foray into Australia. I knew they had big resources and a broad scope, and that they followed through on that. Then I read the scripts and a synopsis of the second and third episodes. I thought it was interesting and it was something I was not really known for. I did a supernatural drama called Glitch more than 10 years ago, but people do not necessarily know me for dramatic acting. That was a bit scary and attractive at the same time.

It is a thriller, and the setup — a desperate father searching for a missing child — is a trope we have seen before. But when I met Christian, the director, and we worked on it more, it became clear that it was very character-driven.

DEADLINE: Given the premise has been done many times before, what do you think sets this apart?

PB: You get the entertainment of the thriller, but you also get a study of the intergenerational trauma affecting two families. It is not simply about heroes and villains. Ian, my character, is not entirely good, and Henry, the ostensibly villainous character played by Brendan Cowell, is not purely dark either.

The moral ambiguity is interesting. Then there is Sarah [Chloe Jean Lourdes], the young girl. When you meet her in the second episode, she does not seem imperilled – she seems quite happy in this family unit. You think you know what the show is going to be, but it becomes something else.

DEADLINE: I wanted to ask you about Colin . In an interview back in July, you were talking about how you were not quite ready to process what the whole show meant. Have you had more time to reflect on what it has done for you and your family?

PB: Being here in the UK helps because the show had an impact here that we did not anticipate at all… So many people saw it on the BBC. I have had a bit more time to reflect and I am starting to feel the legacy of it. ‘Legacy’ is a big word, but there is a feeling that we stopped it at the right time. People were asking, “Are you sure? It is going well. Why would you do that?” But I feel that it was right for various reasons, politically and creatively.

I am really proud of it. The reach has been breathtaking. Harry and I are seeing people responding to the third season and the ending on social media, and it has been received incredibly well. We were nervous because it has been so important to us. We put everything into it and wanted to land the plane well.

DEADLINE: It is a very British thing to end a comedy after two or three seasons, Patrick.

INTERVIEWEE: Absolutely. I understand why. In America, writers’ rooms can keep a show going for a long time. With us, Harry and I write everything, and it is exhausting. That is why I understand shows such as The Office and Fawlty Towers ending when they did. Catastrophe went for four seasons, I think, and its creators were exhausted by the end. You want to continue because you love the show so much, but there is a limit.

DEADLINE: Looking ahead, would you want to write something as closely entwined with your personal life as Colin ?

PB: Colin emerged organically. It is definitely a fictionalised version of us, although the setup is pure fiction. In the writing of the three seasons, we stole elements from our own lives and from other people — friends, stories we had heard. It became a patchwork.

I do not think we would write something exactly like this again. The success of the show is not just that Harry and I write it; it is the setup. It is about a relationship, comedy and love. We will not write another romantic comedy because we have done that, and we would just be trying to repeat ourselves. Every story arises organically once you inhabit it, and this is where we found this one. We got lucky, really.

DEADLINE: The dog being hit by the car is such an immediate device. You instantly understand what kind of world the show is in.

PB: Comedy is hard to set up, and that was a very helpful device. When we were writing the first season, Harry came in one morning and said, “We do not need a dog. We will get an old lady.” She had been allergic to the idea of making a cute dog show. She said, “It is an old lady. She has dementia. She does not know where she is.” We talked about making a statement about how we treat older people.

We told our long-suffering producers, Rob [Gibson] and Ian [Collie]. A couple of days later they came back and said, “We trust you guys. If that is what it is, let us go for it.” Then we said, “No, we have let it go. That was a stupid idea.” For a day and a half, we were making a show in which an old lady, rather than a dog, was hit by a car. It would have been a very different show. Rob and Ian must have gone home wondering what on earth was happening.

DEADLINE: What was the experience of working with Apple compared with Colin ?

PB: It was very different for me. I am across everything on Colin . On Last Seen , I had the luxury of just being an actor. I was responsible for my own character, and that is all. It was decadent for me. Apple has the resources, so we had time to shoot. We were not struggling to shoot nine or 12 minutes a day, or constantly facing the light. We had a 100-day shoot, and you can see it. The production value is there. It looks fantastic.

Bonnie Elliott, the director of photography, has a great eye, and Christian is passionate about the show and deserves a lot of credit for balancing an art-house sensibility with the psychological and emotional realism of the story. He grounds what could have been a juggernaut.

DEADLINE: Australia is fascinating as a production community. Some of the best producers in the world are working there, and unsurprising, distinctive shows are emerging, but it is still often seen as a production location. How do you feel about the state of the Australian industry?

INTERVIEWEE: I think we are in a pretty good spot, although there is never enough work to go around. I have worked on many sets in America, and they are very good at what they do. But there is a sense of “another day, another dollar” — a workaday mentality. In Australia, it is more like, “We are making this thing. Let us all muck in.” That is why Australian crews are the best in the world. Nothing is a problem. Even when there are clearly many problems, we will solve them.

If the new Apple show goes well, hopefully Apple will invest in more Australian stories. There are quotas for streamers, which is a good thing, although I do not think the same quotas are in place for local broadcasters. Streamers may end up carrying the lion’s share of Australian content.

Hollywood productions coming in are good for the industry because the crews get work, but the stories are not Australian and the vernacular is not Australian. That is what I love about Colin : Harry and were are committed to making it genuinely Australian. We do not want to gild the lily. That is how we talk, and people should know that.

DEADLINE: What is next for you? Is it more acting, writing or both?

PB: Ideally, both. I am not great at planning. Harry and I have a film that we are writing for a British production company, but it is early days and I cannot say much about it. That is all we have on the books at the moment. We have two little girls under five, so our family is the priority. We have to make everything work around that.

DEADLINE: What was the experience of making Devil Wears Prada 2 like?

PB: I had a lot of pressure around it because it was an iconic property and people had a strong connection with the original film and those characters. My approach was to stay relaxed and present, and the character was not especially complicated or a huge stretch, so I enjoyed it. Even though it was a massive movie, the set was often very relaxed. There were a couple of days when people gathered in the street to watch, which was strange.

DEADLINE: With the success of Colin and Last Seen , are you still talking to Australian broadcasters, or are global streamers now the main folk competing for your time?

INTERVIEWEE: Harry and I live in Los Angeles, so we are exposed to global opportunities. That is part of the reason we are there. We are still talking about smaller shows, but we ask whether they will travel and whether they have global distributors. I do not want to make something that only goes on a local broadcaster and then sits there. Shows such as Fisk demonstrate that Australian work can travel.

It is ultimately about the quality of the material. When we were pitching Colin , we knocked on every door — although at the time that meant about four doors. The ABC developed it for a short time and then passed. A few other places did the same. Then Binge launched. We saw that it had bought the HBO catalogue and had shows such as The White Lotus and Game of Thrones . Beggars cannot be choosers, and nobody else wanted us, and Binge picked us up. We were very grateful. They were incredible because they gave us the space to make the show we wanted to make. A lot of credit goes to Brian Walsh, one of the commissioners [who passed away in 2023 ]. He is a legend and a person who genuinely loved what he did.

DEADLINE: Brian was one of the most generous executives when I was a young reporter , happy to explain how the international distribution system worked and how Australian television was received around the world.

PB: He was incredibly generous. He was not trying to get to the next thing. He was present in his work and loved what he did. He was the real deal. It is interesting that Alison [Hurbert-Burns, Walsh’s former colleague at Binge] and Bruna [Papandrea] have now set up a company focused on Australian stories . I am delighted for them. Bruna is fantastic, and Alison is a wonderful producer with a great eye.

DEADLINE: How do you see the future of Australian television, particularly with local-content quotas?

PB: Apple, Netflix and the other streamers would prefer quotas not to exist. That is their position around the world, but having quotas is good because it forces them to decide whether they are in or out, and most of them have said they are in. It anchors the industry and gives people some sense of what will happen several years from now. The same is true culturally. It allows Apple, Netflix and Prime Video to have local offices with Australians working in them.

If you do not anchor people in a territory, you get a purely hyper-capitalist model in which the bottom line leads everything. An American executive may say they want something from Australia and send Americans to make an Australian show. You end up with a red-dirt kangaroo version of Australia rather than something genuine.

"会场墙上，用英语和意大利语说明了艺术家挑选的57个日期（扫描尿布二维码后显示出的日期也属于其中之一）以及选择这些理由，正如艺术家在采访中所说的那样，以“I”为主语，以“feel”为谓语。但字体的颜色很淡，阅读起来颇为费劲。扫描阿子酱尿布上的二维码所显示的日期是1919年3月1日，即韩国的三一独立运动纪念日（在韩国称为三一节/三一运动）。墙上的说明里仅写着“I feel determined to remember this significant day for the Korean Independece movement”，通过在网上即刻检索，我了解到这是当时在日本殖民统治下的朝鲜半岛上，33名民族代表宣读《独立宣言书》为契机而爆发的规模最大的非暴力反日独立运动。二维码跳转后显示的石井ゆかり创作的诗作也是以“自由与革命”为主题（就我个人而言，觉得这首诗有些多余）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中，也有人抱着婴儿聚精会神地观看荒川Nash医与斋藤玲儿合作的影像作品《Twins’ First Films》（2026），作品中记录了荒川Nash与双胞胎用iPad看电影的场景；也有人注意到了日本馆1995年代表艺术家崔在垠（Jae-Eun Choi）的作品《Cycle》（1995/2007），该作品投影在墙上凿出的洞穴尽头（其存在感之微妙，让人忍不住想特意用上“注意到”这个词）；还有人仔细阅读墙上的日期。不过，特别是体验抱婴儿的许多参与者，都开心地在空间内四处走动、玩着换尿布过家家，在一轮自拍结束后便下楼归还婴儿，转而前往下一个心仪的展馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而直到最后，我内心的复杂情绪也未曾消散。甚至可以说，反而更加强烈了。怀抱里的终究只是由塑料和布料制成的、沉甸甸且不会动弹的阿子酱，是不可能产生移情（empathy）的。它不会不顾你的方便而哭泣、不会向后挺起身体索求什么，而且很显然，万一不小心掉落也不会受伤。阿子酱的脸上沾着一块白色的污渍，我用衬衫袖子用力擦拭也擦不掉，只好作罢。抱着阿子酱到处走动的体验与真正的育儿之间，存在着一条无论如何也无法填补的巨大鸿沟。然而或许，正是这条巨大的鸿沟，才是社会对于育儿等照料劳动及其承担者的真实写照。这条鸿沟究竟该如何填补？至少，只有这样的疑问留到了最后，这是确凿无疑的。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
赤ちゃん人形を返却したあとで──ヴェネチア・ビエンナーレ日本館「草の赤ちゃん、月の赤ちゃん」【EDITOR’S NOTES】

「あこちゃん」と呼ぶことにした5キロの赤ちゃん人形を抱きかかえ、おむつを替える──その体験は、ケアへの想像力をどこまで開くのか。ヴェネチア・ビエンナーレ開幕前に日本館代表作家、荒川ナッシュ医にインタビューした筆者が現地での体験をレポートする。

今月初旬、ヴェネチア・ビエンナーレを訪れた。滞在時間は約1.5日という弾丸だったが、どうしても荒川ナッシュ医の日本館を見ておきたかった（話題のオーストリア館は残念ながら閉まっていた）。

オンラインミーティングを終えてジャルディーニに到着したのは、オープンから1時間が経過した午前11時ごろ。学校の課外活動でやってきたと思われる小学生や高校生の団体、欧米の観光客など、会場にはすでに多くの来場者が集まっていた。結局のところオープニング以外は正式に開くことのなかったロシア館（しかし扉には映像作品が投影されており、窓越しには展示物が見えた）を通り過ぎ、日本館に到着すると、すでに「抱っこ待ち」の行列ができていた。列をなす人々は、明らかに期待に胸を膨らませている。一方の私は、開催前の作家本人へのインタビューを経てもなお、抱っこしたい気持ちが芽生えるのだろうかという不安と冷ややかさの入り混じる複雑な気持ちが拭えなかった。しかし、とにかく体験してみないことにはわからない。

日本館のピロティで「赤ちゃん捌き」を担当していた若い女性に、「あなたはこの子ね」と指差しであてがわれたのは、褐色の肌の赤ちゃんだった。抱き上げると、聞いていた通りずっしりと重い。どうやって重量を出しているの？ と尋ねると、その若い女性は「お腹に砂の袋を入れてるの」と教えてくれた。よっこらしょ、と抱く体勢を整えると、我が子を抱っこしていたときの感覚が身体の中から勝手に蘇る。ふと、娘がまだ「赤ちゃん」に属する月齢から一緒に育ち、どこに行くにも連れ回していた赤ちゃん人形の「あこちゃん」を思い出したが、当時の娘にとって、あこちゃんは（お腹に砂は入っていなかったけれど）とても重かったのかもしれない。日本館内で暮らす約200体の赤ちゃんたちの例に漏れず、私のあこちゃん（ここからはそう呼ぶことにする）もJINSから提供されたミラーレンズのサングラスをかけていたが、そこに映る微妙な表情の自分に気づき、思わず苦笑いがこぼれた。

階段を上り上階に到着すると、赤ちゃん抱っこを楽しみながら、空間中に設置された赤ちゃんたちを眺める参加者たちの、どこか浮き足だった様子に対し、複雑な気持ちを抱えたままの自分に居心地の悪さを感じる。インタビューで「赤ちゃんのかわいさや純粋さが、出産や子育てをめぐる様々な問題を覆い隠し、無批判な共感を強いる可能性もあるのでは？」と作家に聞いた際、本人も「アミューズメントパーク的なかわいさ」一色になる懸念を打ち明けた上で、かわいさだけでは語れない両義的な感情に場を開き、人形のリアルな重さもそのために作用してほしいと話してくれたが、私の目の前に広がっていたのは、リアリティに欠けた「ごっこ遊び」の世界だった。おむつに付されたQRコードを読み込もうと、皆、嬉々としておむつ替えの台を目指しているが、実際におむつを完全に取り外し、丁寧におしりを拭き、新しいものに交換するわけではない。ここで体験できるのは、あくまで「ふり」だ。気持ちの乗らない自分を鼓舞し、わたしもやってみたが、硬直し空を見るあこちゃんになぜか申し訳ない気持ちになり、QRコードの写メが終わるとコソコソとオムツを元通りに締め直した。

会場の壁には、作家が選んだ57の日付（オムツのQRコードを読み込んだ先に表示される日付も、このうちのどれかだ）と、それらを選んだ理由が、作家がインタビューで話していた通り、「I」を主語、「feel」を述語として、英語とイタリア語で説明されていたが、文字の色が薄く、読むのに苦労した。あこちゃんのおむつに付されたQRコードを読み込んで現れた日付は、1919年3月1日、韓国の三一独立運動（サミル独立運動）記念日（韓国では三一節 / 三一運動）だった。壁の説明には、「I feel determined to remember this significant day for the Korean Independece movement」とだけ書かれてあり、ネットですぐに調べると、当時、日本の植民地支配下にあった朝鮮半島で33人の民族代表が「独立宣言書」を朗読したことをきっかけに始まった、最大規模の非暴力・反日独立運動のことだとわかった。QRコードの先に表示される石井ゆかりによる詩も、「自由と革命」がテーマだった（個人的に、この詩は蛇足だと感じた）。

中には、会場入り口に設置されたモニターに映る、荒川ナッシュと双子がiPadで映画を見る様子を映した荒川ナッシュ医と斎藤玲児による映像作品《Twins’ First Films》（2026）を赤ちゃんを抱えながら熱心に見る人、壁にくり抜かれた穴の先に投影される1995年の日本館代表作家、チェ・ジェウン（Jae-Eun Choi）による《Cycle》（1995／2007）に気づく人（「気づく」という表現をあえて選びたくなるほどさりげなく存在している）、あるいは、壁の日付を丁寧に読む人もいたが、とくに赤ちゃん抱っこを体験する参加者の多くは、楽しそうに空間内を歩き回り、オムツ替えごっこをし、セルフィーがひと通り終わると階下に降り、赤ちゃんを返却して次のお目当てパビリオンに移動していった。

しかし最後まで、私自身の複雑な気持ちが消えることはなかった。むしろ、強まったとさえ言える。自分の腕の中にいるのはあくまでプラスチックと布でできた、ずっしり動かぬあこちゃんであり、感情移入などできるはずがない。こちらの都合とは無関係に泣いたりのけぞったりして何かを求めてはこないし、万が一落っことしても怪我しないのは明らかだ。あこちゃんの顔には白い汚れがついていたが、シャツの袖でゴシゴシ拭いても落ちなかったので諦めた。あこちゃんを抱き抱え、歩き回る体験と本当の育児のあいだには、埋めようにも埋まらない巨大な溝がある。しかしもしかすると、その巨大な溝こそが、子育てをはじめとするケアという労働やその担い手に対する、社会のリアルなのかもしれない。その溝はどう埋めることができるのか。少なくとも、そんな問いだけが最後まで残ったのは確かだ。

article_text:
Rubaiya Qatar, a new quadrennial opening next month in Doha, has announced the full list of artists participating in its first edition. The quadrennial will include over 120 artists across three exhibitions and public art installations.

The quadrennial’s inaugural edition, Unruly Waters, will be curated by Tom Eccles , executive director of the Center for Curatorial Studies and the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College; Ruba Katrib , chief curator and director of curatorial affairs at MoMA PS1; Mark Rappolt , editor-in-chief of ArtReview and ArtReview Asia ; and Shabbir Husain Mustafa , chief curator at Singapore Art Museum.

Unruly Waters )وحُمُ جُُ ياه(م , will take place from 21 November to 30 April and will feature:

Bani Abidi, Pakistan; Nicholas Galanin , United States; Lawrence Abu Hamdan , Lebanon / UK; Shilpa Gupta , India; Yousef Ahmad, Qatar; Hit Man Gurung, Nepal; Khalid Albaih, Sudan; Mayar Hamdan, Palestine; Kamal Aljafari, Palestine; Sohrab Hura , India; Sophia Al-Maria , Qatar; Saodat Ismailova , Uzbekistan; Farah Al Qasimi , UAE; Naiza Khan, UK / Pakistan; Majid Al-Remaihi, Qatar; Saba Khan, Pakistan; Shaima Al-Tamimi, Yemen; Ayoung Kim , South Korea; Meriem Bennani , Morocco; Charles Lim, Singapore; Mohamed Bourouissa , France / Algeria; Imaad Majeed, Sri Lanka; Liu Chuang, China; Diego Marcon , Italy; Ade Darmawan, Indonesia; Naeem Mohaiemen , Bangladesh; Alia Farid , Puerto Rico / Kuwait; Yuko Mohri , Japan; Simone Fattal , Lebanon; Manny Montelibano, Philippines; Cao Fei , China; Jean Katambayi Mukendi, DRC; Oscar Murillo , Colombia; Selma Selman, Bosnia and Herzegovina; Hira Nabi, Pakistan; Priya Sen, India; Dala Nasser, Lebanon; Wael Shawky, Egypt; New Red Order, United States; Ahlam Shibli, Palestine; Ho Tzu Nyen , Singapore; Marina Tabassum, Bangladesh; Lydia Ourahmane, Algeria; Newsha Tavakolian, Iran; Pratchaya Phinthong , Thailand; Nathalie Vairac, France / Senegal; Tan Pin Pin, Singapore; Adrian van Wyk, South Africa; Khalil Rabah Palestine; Munem Wasif , Bangladesh; Sheelasha Rajbhandari, Nepal; He Xiangyu, China; Araya Rasdjarmrearnsook, Thailand; Ayman Zedani, Saudi Arabia.

Our Common Currents (حِينَ نَنْسَابُ معًا) will take place from 22 November to 30 April, curated by Lina Patmali, Acting Head of Curatorial Affairs for Rubaiya Qatar, and feature:

Nadia Belerique, Canada; Basim Magdy, Egypt and Aziz Motawa, Kuwait; Joseph Ntensibe, Uganda; works from the Art Mill Museum Collection by KABINDA; Olafur Eliasson, Iceland / Denmark; Barbara Chase-Riboud, France / US; Lala Rukh, Pakistan and new commissions by Taloi Havini, Australia / Bougainville; Latent Community, Greece; Miguel Fernández de Castro, Mexico; Artcom Platform, Kazakhstan.

Seething Sea (بَحْرٌ مَسْجُورٍ), curated by Wadha Al-Aqeedi, a curator at Qatar Museums, will take place from 22 November to 30 April and feature:

Abbas Al-Mahroos, Bahrain; Hisham Zubari, Bahrain; Abdul Karim Al-Bosta, Bahrain; Hossein Kashian, Iran; Abdul Qader Al-Rais, United Arab Emirates; Iran Darroudi, Iran; Abdulhalim Radwi, Saudi Arabia; Issa Saqer, Kuwait; Abdulkarim Al-Orrayed, Bahrain; Jasem AlSanea, Kuwait; Abdullah Al-Muharraqi, Bahrain; Jassim Zaini, Qatar; Abdulrasoul Salman, Kuwait; Khaled Al-Rahhal, Iraq; Abeer Al-Kuwari, Qatar; Khalifa Al-Qattan, Kuwait; Ahmed Abdul Ridha Saleh, Kuwait; Mahmoud Sabri, Iraq; Ali Dasmal Al-Kuwari, Qatar; Mahood Ahmad, Iraq; Ali Sharif, Qatar; Majid Hilal Al-Naimi, Qatar; Ali Yahya, Iraq; Manal AlDowayan, Saudi Arabia; Alymamah Rashed, Kuwait; Massoud Arabshahi, Iran; Amna Al-Baker, Qatar; Mohammed Fadhil, Oman; Bahman Dadkhah, Iran; Mohammed Ghani Hikmet, Iraq; Balqees Fakhro, Bahrain; Mohammed Jassim Al-Jaidah, Qatar; Basmah Felemban, Saudi Arabia; Monira Al Qadiri, Kuwait; Charles Hossein-Zenderoudi, Iran; Moosa Omar Al-Zadjali, Oman; Dalal Al-Obaidi, Kuwait; Nasser Ovissi, Iran; Dia Azzawi, Iraq; Pouran Jinchi, Iran; Essa Al-Ghanem, Qatar; Rafa Nasiri, Iraq; Essa Al-Malki, Qatar; Salem Mathkour, Iraq; Faisal Samra, Saudi Arabia; Sophia Al-Maria, Qatar; Fuad Al-Futaih, Yemen; Suad Al-Attar, Iraq; Gholamhossein Nami, Iran; Tamader Al-Sultan, Qatar; Hamid Al-Attar, Iraq; Wafika Sultan Al-Essa, Qatar; Hassan Sharif, United Arab Emirates.

Newly commissioned public art installations will be unveiled between 21 November and 30 April. Artists include:

Rirkrit Tiravanija , Thailand; Jitish Kallat , India; Ibrahim Mahama , Ghana; Lubna Chowdhary, UK; Minerva Cuevas, Mexico; Shaikha Hala Al Khalifa, Bahrain; Nazgol Ansarinia, Iran.
